notes.meaning: The leaders had asked Jesus who gave Him the right to act as He did. He answers with one question of His own. He is not dodging. If they answer honestly, their answer will also answer their own question. Jesus had already shown His authority through His many miracles.

"John's baptism" stands for John the Baptist's whole work, both his preaching and his baptizing. If the leaders said John was sent by God, they would have to believe him. And John had pointed to Jesus as the promised Savior. So they did not ask what was true. They only weighed their own reputation and safety. Luke adds that they feared the crowd would stone them.

"We do not know" was really a lie. The honest words would have been "We will not tell." Because they would not admit what they knew, Jesus would not explain His authority again. He had often told them before, and they had not believed. People who bury the truth they already know are not given more.

Jesus starts a story with a question, so the leaders will judge themselves. The father stands for God, who calls all people to work in His vineyard. Working there means doing what God asks, because true faith shows in how we live. The word "today" means God wants us to obey now.

The first son rudely says no and gives no excuse at all. Later he is sorry, changes his mind, and goes. He pictures open sinners, like tax collectors, who at first refused God but turned back when John and Jesus preached. The proof that he had truly changed was that he went.

The second son answers politely, "I will, sir," but he never goes. He pictures the scribes and Pharisees. They claimed to be eager to serve God, but their actions said the opposite. Saying and doing are two different things.

The leaders give the right answer, and without seeing it they condemn themselves. Jesus says that tax collectors and prostitutes are already going into God's kingdom ahead of them. He does not excuse those people's sins. His point is that they turned from their sins, while the leaders never did.

John came "in a righteous way." He taught what was right, and he lived it too. Sinners truly believed him, which means they gave their lives to God and did not just agree in words. The leaders watched these lives change and still would not turn back to God. That made their stubbornness even worse.

This story is built on the vineyard song in Isaiah 5. The landowner is God, and the vineyard is His people Israel. The wall shows His protection, and the tenants are the priests and religious leaders. Not every detail needs a special meaning. Together they show how much care God took over His people.

In those days, rent was often paid with part of the harvest. The servants stand for the prophets God sent to Israel. The fruit God wanted was obedience to His ways. He was not asking for anything unfair.

This is what really happened to God's prophets. Jeremiah was beaten. Zechariah was stoned to death in the temple. Others were killed. The worst attacks often came from the very leaders who claimed to serve God.
God did not give up. He kept sending messengers, even more than before. This shows how patient He is. It also shows how stubborn the tenants were, since nothing God did changed them.

The son is Jesus Himself. Here He sets Himself apart from all the prophets as God's own Son. Sending His only, much-loved Son shows God's great love. God knew what would happen. The story simply uses human words to show how terrible it was to reject Him.

The tenants knew exactly who the son was and planned to kill him anyway. In the same way, the leaders saw Jesus as a threat to their power and wanted Him out of the way. God's inheritance truly belongs to His Son. Wanting to be masters instead of servants lies at the root of sin.

Jesus is pointing to His own coming death, just days away. They threw the son out of the vineyard. In the same way, Jesus was crucified outside the city gate of Jerusalem. The Romans carried it out, but the leaders were held responsible.

Jesus lets His hearers decide the punishment, so that they judge themselves. Their answer has a play on words, something like "He will bring those bad men to a bad end." The sources see this fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem about forty years later. God will always have people who bear fruit for Him. Luke says they also cried "God forbid!" once they saw the story was about them.

Jesus quotes Psalm 118, the same psalm the crowds used when they shouted "Hosanna." The builders are the chief priests and leaders. They threw aside the very stone God chose. The cornerstone is the main stone that holds a building together. Jesus became the foundation of His church. This was first true in a way of King David, and fully true of Jesus. It is God's doing and a wonder to see.

The special privileges of God's kingdom would be taken from these leaders and the nation that followed them. They would be given to a people who bear fruit, mostly non-Jewish believers. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that this lasts until "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11). Calvin says it also warns us not to grow proud. The fruit means the fruit of the Spirit, a changed life.

Those who stumble over Jesus and refuse Him only hurt themselves. Those on whom the stone falls in judgment are crushed to dust, like chaff blown by the wind. The sources link this to the fall of Jerusalem and to the final judgment. Some old copies of Matthew leave this verse out, but the same words appear in Luke 20:18.
The leaders understood that both stories, the two sons and the tenants, were about them. A guilty conscience needs no one to point the finger. But instead of turning back to God, they grew angry.

Only their fear of the crowds held them back, just as it had about John in verse 26. The people saw Jesus as a prophet, though not yet as the Messiah. God has ways of holding back wicked people and protecting His own until His time comes.
